extraction.name: CommonsenseQA
extraction.description: A challenging new dataset for commonsense question answering containing 12,247 multiple-choice questions that require prior knowledge and common sense to answer. Questions are generated by extracting concepts from ConceptNet that share the same semantic relation to a source concept, and crowd-workers author questions that discriminate between these concepts.
extraction.creator: Alon Talmor, Jonathan Herzig, Nicholas Lourie, Jonathan Berant
extraction.publisher: Tel-Aviv University, Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were generated through a crowdsourcing process where workers were shown a question concept and three answer concepts from ConceptNet that share the same semantic relation. Workers authored three questions per concept set, where each question contains the question concept and has one of the answer concepts as the correct answer while the other two are incorrect. Workers then added two additional distractors per question: one selected from ConceptNet and one manually formulated.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Data was extracted from ConceptNet, a graph knowledge-base containing 32 million triplets where nodes represent natural language concepts and edges represent commonsense relations. The extraction process filtered triplets to 236,208 based on relation types, concept length, language, and edit distance, resulting in approximately 130,000 triplets (43,000 question sets) for question generation.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: ConceptNet triplets were filtered using the following steps: (1) Filtered triplets with general relations (e.g., RelatedTo) or relations already well-explored in NLP (e.g., IsA), using 22 relations in total; (2) Filtered triplets where one of the concepts is more than four words or not in English; (3) Filtered triplets where the edit distance between concepts is too low. This resulted in 236,208 triplets from which question sets were created by grouping three different triplets with the same question concept and relation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd-workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) were shown a question concept and three answer concepts for each question set. They formulated three questions where all questions contain the question concept and each question has one of the answer concepts as the correct answer but not the other two. Workers were instructed to avoid using words that have a strong relation to the answer concept. Workers then added two additional distractors per question: one selected from ConceptNet answer concepts with the same relation, and one manually formulated to seem plausible but easy for humans to dismiss. Only annotators with at least 75% of questions passing verification were accepted.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Each question was verified by 2 workers from a disjoint group of verifiers. Verifiers annotated questions as unanswerable or chose the right answer. Only questions verified by at least one worker that answered correctly were used. This verification process filtered out 15% of the questions.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Analysis of 100 development set examples showed that the BERT-LARGE baseline struggles with several categories: examples involving negation or understanding antonyms (42.8% accuracy), examples requiring factoid knowledge (38.4% accuracy), questions where the correct answer has finer granularity compared to distractors (35.4% accuracy), and cases where the correct answer needs to meet a conjunction of conditions while distractors meet only one (23.8% accuracy). Learning curves suggest that even with 100k examples, BERT-LARGE accuracy would be roughly 75%, still substantially lower than human performance of 88.9%.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for training and evaluating question answering systems that require commonsense knowledge. The data is split into training/development/test sets with an 80/10/10 split. Two types of splits are provided: (a) random split where questions are split uniformly at random, and (b) question concept split where each set has disjoint question concepts. The random split is considered the primary split as it is harder for models.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Each question was verified by 2 workers. For human evaluation, 100 random questions were sampled and each received answers from 5 workers (taking majority vote).
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: 122 formulators contributed to question generation, with 10 workers formulating more than 85% of the questions. Only annotators with at least 75% of questions passing verification were accepted. A disjoint group of workers was trained to verify the generated questions.
